difficultyRationale: The self-invocation pitfall is one of the most frequently misdiagnosed Spring bugs in production code, and testing it requires understanding proxy-based AOP, not just the annotation's intent.
prompt: Inside `OrderService`, the non-transactional method `placeOrder()` calls `this.saveOrder(order)` directly, where `saveOrder()` is annotated `@Transactional`. Both methods live in the same class, and the project uses Spring's default proxy-based AOP (no AspectJ compile-time or load-time weaving is configured). When `placeOrder()` invokes `saveOrder()` this way, what actually happens?
explanation: Spring's default AOP implementation works by wrapping the bean in a proxy; advice such as the transaction interceptor only runs when a call arrives *through that proxy*. A call made as `this.saveOrder(...)` from inside the same object goes directly to the real method, never passing through the proxy, so `@Transactional` has no effect on it — the method runs with whatever transaction (if any) was already active on the caller's thread.

options.text: Spring transparently routes the self-invocation through the proxy anyway, exactly as it would if an external caller invoked `saveOrder()` on the injected bean reference, because the container rewrites `this` references inside managed beans.
options.explanation: This is the common misconception. A self-invocation via `this` never reaches the proxy; only calls that come in from outside the bean (through the reference other beans were injected with) go through it.

options.text: `saveOrder()` runs with no transaction managed by this annotation at all, because `this.saveOrder(...)` bypasses the proxy entirely — the advice only applies when an external caller invokes the method through the bean's proxy reference.
options.explanation: Correct. This is exactly the self-invocation pitfall: the annotation is silently ignored for internal calls under default proxy-based AOP.

options.text: Spring Boot fails application startup with a `BeanCreationException`, since the container's bean-validation pass detects the self-invocation pattern statically and explicitly rejects it as invalid `@Transactional` configuration before the context finishes loading.
options.explanation: There is no such startup check. The code compiles and runs fine; it just silently does not get the transactional behavior the developer expected, which is what makes this bug hard to notice.

options.text: Spring detects the self-invocation through bytecode analysis at class-loading time and weaves the transaction advice directly into the compiled method body, making a proxy unnecessary.
options.explanation: That describes AspectJ compile-time or load-time weaving, which the question explicitly rules out. Without it, Spring's default mechanism is proxy-based, and a proxy cannot intercept a call that never passes through it.
